definition.text: The branch of welfare economics that studies how individual preferences can be combined into good collective decisions.

facts.text: It is normative, asking how a society should decide, unlike political science, which describes how societies actually decide.
Constitutions, parliamentary voting procedures and electoral systems are real-world social choice rules, so the field is sometimes called voting theory.
It began with the Marquis de Condorcet; Kenneth Arrow's book Social Choice and Individual Values opened its modern era.
Two classic rules are the utilitarian rule, which maximizes the sum of utilities, and the egalitarian or Rawlsian rule, which maximizes the smallest utility.
Gibbard's theorem shows that with three or more outcomes no voting rule can always make honest voting the best strategy.
In 1970 Amartya Sen's Collective Choice and Social Welfare brought comparisons between people and the idea of capability into the field.
Later work extended social choice to fair division, legal compensation and natural resources, among other topics.

definition.text: The finding that majority voting over three or more options can go round in a circle: A beats B, B beats C, yet C beats A.

facts.text: It shows democracy cannot simply equal majority rule, which becomes self-contradictory with three or more options.
With only two options, May's theorem shows simple majority is the best rule.
A review of 37 studies covering 265 real elections found 25 cases of the paradox, a likelihood of 9.4%.

title: Interpersonal utility comparison

definition.text: The disputed question of whether one person's gain or loss in well-being can be measured and weighed against another's.

facts.text: Following Bentham, utilitarians argue utilities can be compared and added up into a total for society to maximize.
Diminishing marginal utility has been used to justify transfers from rich to poor, since the poor gain more from an extra unit of income.
Lionel Robbins argued such comparisons are unscientific and cannot be tested.
Harsanyi and Sen reply that at least partial comparisons are possible, so social choice should proceed on that basis.

contested_note: Robbins and his followers deny that utility can be compared across people, while Harsanyi and Sen argue partial comparison is possible.

definition.text: An imaginary decision-maker used in economic models who chooses everyone's allocations to maximize a social welfare function.

facts.text: The planner's problem is a constrained optimization; solving it for every set of weights on people yields all Pareto efficient allocations.
Solving it would require knowing everyone's preferences and every resource limit, so economists ask whether decentralized markets can reach the same outcomes; the welfare theorems answer this.
Ramsey first framed his growth model as a social planner maximizing total consumption across generations.

definition.text: The gap a tax opens between the price buyers pay and the price sellers receive for a good.

facts.text: With a tax, consumers pay more, suppliers receive less, and the quantity traded falls; the price gap equals the per-unit tax.
The wedge-shaped area on a supply-and-demand diagram equals the deadweight loss of the tax, one half times the tax times the fall in quantity.
A monopoly pricing above marginal cost drives a similar wedge between what consumers pay and what it costs to supply.

definition.text: Who actually bears the cost of a tax, which may differ from who legally hands the money to the government.

facts.text: Statutory incidence falls on whoever pays the government; economic incidence falls on whoever really bears the cost, and the first does not determine the second.
Economic incidence depends entirely on the elasticities of supply and demand: the side less able to adjust bears more.
Smokers bear most of a tobacco tax because their demand barely responds to price, while owners of beachfront hotels bear most of a hotel tax because supply cannot change.
In the long run supply and demand become more elastic, so the split of the burden can shift.

definition.text: The result that when one condition for an ideal economy cannot be met, the best remaining option may require moving other conditions away from their ideal values too.

facts.text: Richard Lipsey and Kelvin Lancaster showed this in 1956.
If one market distortion cannot be removed, adding another distortion in a linked market may partly offset it and raise efficiency.
Fixing a market failure in one sector while an uncorrectable failure remains in a related sector can lower overall efficiency.
A common error, the 'fallacy of exhaustive effort', assumes meeting as many remaining ideal conditions as possible gives the second-best result.
Example: liberalising trade while ignoring an environmental externality, because 'free trade is good', can leave welfare lower than doing nothing.
When the externality itself cannot be taxed, taxing a related product can be the second-best Pigouvian solution.
